source_reference: Liang, Song, and Yuan, Decentralized Optimization over Time-Varying Row-Stochastic Digraphs, arXiv:2512.24483v1 (Theorem 2)

problem.description: Decentralized optimization over a time-varying broadcast network; each objective function f_i is accessible only by node i.

assumptions.name: B_tilde_strongly_connected_graph_sequence
assumptions.math: \{G^{(k)}=(V,E^{(k)})\}_{k\ge 0}\text{ satisfies the following: there exists an integer }\tilde B>0\text{ such that for any }k\ge 0,\text{ the }\tilde B\text{-step accumulated graph }G_k^{\tilde B}:=\left(V,\bigcup_{l=k}^{k+\tilde B-1}E^{(l)}\right)\text{ is strongly connected. Additionally, each graph }G^{(k)}\text{ contains a self-loop at every node.}

assumptions.name: rapidly_changing_broadcast_network
assumptions.math: \text{For each }k\ge 0\text{ and }i\in[n],\text{ node }i\text{ does not know its out-degree }d_i^{\mathrm{out},(k)}\text{ in graph }G^{(k)}.\text{ Additionally, for each }k\ge 0,\text{ the mixing matrix generated from }G^{(k)}\text{ can only be used once.}

assumptions.name: compatible_row_stochastic_mixing
assumptions.math: a_{ij}>0\text{ if }(j\to i)\in E,\text{ and }a_{ij}=0\text{ otherwise.}\quad A1_n=1_n.

assumptions.name: lower_bounded_entries
assumptions.math: \text{Suppose that for each }k\ge 0,\text{ we have a mixing matrix }A^{(k)}\text{ that is compatible with }G^{(k)}.\text{ There exists a scalar }\tau>0\text{ such that all nonzero entries of }A^{(k)}\text{ satisfy }a_{ij}^{(k)}\ge \tau\text{ for all }k\ge 0.

assumptions.name: smoothness
assumptions.math: \text{There exist constants }L,\Delta\ge 0\text{ such that for all }i\in[n]\text{ and all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d,\quad \|\nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|,\quad\text{and}\quad f_i(x^{(0)})-\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d} f_i(x)\le \Delta.

assumptions.name: theorem2_uniform_PULM_mixing_rate
assumptions.math: \text{there exists }C_W>0\text{ and }0\le \beta_W<1\text{ such that }\|W^{(k,r)}-n^{-1}1_n1_n^\top\|_2\le C_W\beta_W^r\text{ for all }k\text{ and }r.

assumptions.name: lemma1_local_row_stochastic_sequence
assumptions.math: \text{For a sequence of row-stochastic matrices }\tilde A^{(1)},\tilde A^{(2)},\cdots\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}

assumptions.name: algorithm1_initialization_and_diagonal_anchor
assumptions.math: W^{(0)}=I_n.\quad W^{(k+\frac12)}=A^{(k)}W^{(k)};\quad \text{Replace the diagonal entries of }W^{(k+\frac12)}\text{ by }\frac1n\text{, and name it }W^{(k+1)};

output.type: local iterates after K outer iterations

main_theorem.statement_math: \text{Suppose Assumption 1, 2 and 3 hold. To simplify the notations, in Algorithm 3 we further assume that there exists }C_W>0\text{ and }0\le\beta_W<1\text{ such that }\|W^{(k,r)}-n^{-1}1_n1_n^\top\|_2\le C_W\beta_W^r\text{ for all }k\text{ and }r.\text{ When }\gamma\le \frac{1}{24nC_W^2L}\text{ and }R_k\ge\max\left\{\frac{\ln(C_W)}{1-\beta_W},\frac{\ln(k)}{1-\beta_W}\right\},\text{ we have }\frac1K\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\|\nabla f(\bar x^{(k)})\|^2\le \frac{18\Delta}{\gamma K},\quad \text{where }\bar x^{(k)}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{(k)}.\text{ By choosing }\gamma=\frac{1}{24nC_W^2L}\text{ and }R_k=\max\left\{\frac{\ln(C_W)}{1-\beta_W},\frac{\ln(k)}{1-\beta_W}\right\}\text{ for all }k\ge0,\text{ we have }\frac1K\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\|\nabla f(\bar x^{(k)})\|^2\le \frac{432nC_W^2L\Delta}{K}.\text{ and the total number of communication rounds equals to }\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}R_k\le \max\left\{\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\frac{\ln(k)}{1-\beta_W},\sum_{k=1}^{K-1}\frac{\ln(C_W)}{1-\beta_W}\right\}=\frac{\max\{K\ln(K),K\ln(C_W)\}}{1-\beta_W}.\text{ In Theorem 2, when we define the total number of communication rounds }T=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}R_k,\text{ we obtain }K=O(T/\ln(T)).\text{ Plugging this into (5) results in an overall convergence rate of }O\left(\frac{\ln(T)}{T}\right).
main_theorem.rate: O(ln(T)/T) in total communication rounds T, via K=O(T/ln(T)) and the O(1/K) averaged stationarity bound.
main_theorem.measure: Averaged squared norm of the centralized gradient at the network mean iterate, \frac1K\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\|\nabla f(\bar x^{(k)})\|^2.

key_lemmas.name: uniform_B_step_mixing
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{Suppose Assumptions 1 and 3 hold. Then there exist an integer }0<B<n\tilde B\text{ and a scalar }\eta\in[\tau^B,1)\text{ such that }\Phi(k+B,k):=\prod_{l=0}^{B-1}A^{(k+l)}\ge \eta,\quad \forall k\ge0.
key_lemmas.role: Provides the uniform positive B-window mixing constant used in Proposition 2 and Theorem 1.

proof.description: Fix starting time k and nodes s,e. If s=e the self-loop gives a trivial trajectory; otherwise initialize the searched set V_ominus={s} and introduce path and timed-transition notation.

Using Assumption 1 over the first tilde-B interval, choose a shortest path s -> v_1 -> ... -> e and a time t_1 in [k,k+tilde B-1] with (s,v_1) in E^(t_1), then construct a transition trajectory staying at s until t_1 and moving to v_1.

Repeat from the new node and next time. If the next shortest-path node is already searched, retrace to the last searched node v_+ and wait until a time t_* when an edge to the first new node v_* appears.

The repetition adds a new node each time and therefore takes no more than n repetitions; Assumption 3 lower bounds the transition probability by tau^{n tilde B}, producing B and eta independent of k and node indices.

key_lemmas.name: linear_convergence_row_stochastic_products
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{For a sequence of row-stochastic matrices }\tilde A^{(1)},\tilde A^{(2)},\cdots\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},\text{ assuming }\tilde A_{i,j}^{(t)}\ge \eta>0,\forall i,j\in[n],\forall t=1,2,\ldots,\text{ we have: }\tilde A_\infty:=\prod_{t=1}^{+\infty}\tilde A^{(t)}\text{ exists, }\tilde A_\infty=1_n\pi^\top,\text{ and }\max\left|\prod_{t=1}^{T}\tilde A^{(t)}-\tilde A_\infty\right|\le \frac{1+\eta}{\eta}(1-\eta)^T.
key_lemmas.role: Converts uniform entrywise positivity into an identical-row product limit with an exponential deviation bound.

proof.description: For an arbitrary vector x^(0) in R^n, introduce the local product iterate x^(t):=\tilde A^(t)\cdots\tilde A^(1)x^(0), then decompose x^(t) into a consensus scalar p^(t) and a nonnegative surplus z^(t) as equation (8).
Expand the recursion through a row-stochastic matrix and define the minimizing index i_* used to update p and z.
For a fixed entry i, split the column indices into nonnegative and negative row-difference subsets.
Using the definition of z^(t+1), expand the i-th entry as a row-difference sum over all columns.
proof.math: 0\le z_i^{(t+1)}=\tilde A_{i,\cdot}^{(t+1)}z^{(t)}-\tilde A_{i_*,\cdot}^{(t+1)}z^{(t)}=\sum_{1\le j\le n}(\tilde A_{i,j}^{(t+1)}-\tilde A_{i_*,j}^{(t+1)})z_j^{(t)}.

proof.description: Restrict the all-column sum to the positive subset J^+, dropping the negative row-difference terms.
proof.math: \sum_{1\le j\le n}(\tilde A_{i,j}^{(t+1)}-\tilde A_{i_*,j}^{(t+1)})z_j^{(t)}\le\sum_{j\in J^+}(\tilde A_{i,j}^{(t+1)}-\tilde A_{i_*,j}^{(t+1)})z_j^{(t)}.

proof.description: Bound each nonnegative z_j^(t) in the J^+ sum by the infinity norm of z^(t).
Rewrite the positive row-difference sum as the difference of two row partial sums and use row-stochasticity with the eta lower bound to get the contraction coefficient.
Take the maximum over entries to obtain the one-step infinity-norm contraction.
Iterate the one-step contraction to get the T-step geometric decay of the surplus.
Bound the increment of p^(t) by the current surplus norm and then by the geometric surplus decay; this is the displayed inequality labeled (9).
Telescope the p-increments from 0 to t and sum the geometric series to prove boundedness of p^(t).
Use z^(t)->0 from the geometric surplus decay and p^(t)->p_tilde from monotone boundedness, then apply this convergence to unit-vector initial data to obtain the product limit with identical rows.
proof.math: \prod_{t=1}^{+\infty}\tilde A^{(t)}=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\tilde A^{(t)}\cdots\tilde A^{(1)}(e_1,\ldots,e_n)=(\tilde p_1 1_n,\ldots,\tilde p_n1_n),\quad \tilde A_\infty=1_n\pi^\top.

proof.description: For the convergence rate, rewrite the product error using the decomposition and the identical-row limit.
proof.math: (\tilde A^{(t)}\cdots\tilde A^{(1)})x^{(0)}-\tilde A_\infty x^{(0)}=x^{(t)}-\tilde p1_n=z^{(t)}+(p^{(t)}-\tilde p)1_n.

proof.description: Bound the tail coefficient \tilde p-p^(t) by summing the p-increment estimate (9) from s=t to infinity.
Combine equation (10), the surplus decay, and the p-tail bound to control the infinite norm of the product error for arbitrary x^(0).
Substitute unit vectors e_j and use ||z^(0)||_infty=1 to get the stated columnwise maximum-deviation bound.

key_lemmas.name: limiting_property
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{For }\{G^{(k)},A^{(k)}\}_{k\ge0}\text{ satisfying Assumptions 1--3, define }\Phi(k+B,k)=\prod_{i=0}^{B-1}A^{(k+i)}.\text{ It follows that }\lim_{k\to\infty}\Phi(k+B,k)=1_n\pi_k^\top,\forall,\text{ where }\pi_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is determined by the sequence }\{A^{(t)}\}_{t\ge k}.\text{ Moreover, the convergence occurs at an exponential rate.}
key_lemmas.role: Explains why ordinary row-stochastic gossip has a future-dependent biased limit, motivating the memory correction.

proof.description: Group the original row-stochastic sequence into B-factor blocks using Proposition 1 so every block has entries at least eta.
Use Lemma 1 on the blocked sequence to obtain a limit with identical rows.
For arbitrary k, decompose the product into a leftover factor and T=floor(k/B) full B-blocks.
Apply Lemma 1's exponential bound to the full blocks.
Bound the total deviation by the leftover factor norm and the full-block deviation.
Use T=floor(k/B)>=k/B-1 to rewrite the rate as an exponential in k and conclude the original product has the same limit.
The proof then shows unpredictability: after any finite prefix, the future product can have arbitrary limit vector pi_k, and the original limit vector is pi_k^T times the prefix product.

key_lemmas.name: submatrix_product_inequality
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{For any }S\text{ row-stochastic matrices }A^{(1)},\ldots,A^{(S)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},\text{ we have }0\le\prod_{s=1}^S A_{-\ell,-\ell}^{(s)}\le\left(\prod_{s=1}^S A^{(s)}\right)_{-\ell,-\ell},\text{ where }M_{-\ell,-\ell}\text{ represents the }(n-1)\times(n-1)\text{ matrix obtained by removing the }\ell\text{-th row and the }\ell\text{-th column of }M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}.
key_lemmas.role: Allows Theorem 1 to compare products of submatrices with submatrices of products.

proof.description: The left inequality follows because nonnegative combinations cannot produce negative elements.
proof.ref: Lemma 2 statement, lines 1265-1272; proof explanation at Appendix B.4, lines 1278-1279

proof.description: It suffices to prove the right inequality for S=2 and then use induction; set ell=1 without loss of generality and block-partition the product.
Expand the lower-right block; the rank-one cross term is entrywise nonnegative, giving the desired inequality.

key_lemmas.name: PULM_average_consensus
key_lemmas.statement_math: \text{For }\{G^{(k)}\}_{k\ge0}\text{ satisfying Assumptions 1 and 2, and }\{A^{(k)}\}_{k\ge0}\text{ satisfying Assumption 3, the following statements hold: }1.\ \text{In Algorithm 1, the sequence }\{\max_{i,j}|[W^{(k)}]_{ij}-n^{-1}|\}_{k\ge0}\text{ is non-increasing. }2.\ \text{In both Algorithms 1 and 2, }\|W^{(K)}-n^{-1}1_n1_n^\top\|_F\le\frac{n}{1-\eta}(1-\eta)^{K/B}.\ 3.\ \text{In Algorithm 2, }\|z^{(K)}-n^{-1}1_n1_n^\top x^{(0)}\|_F\le\frac{n}{1-\eta}(1-\eta)^{K/B}\|x^{(0)}\|_F.\ \text{Here, the constants }B>0\text{ and }\eta\in(0,1)\text{ are defined in Proposition 1.}
key_lemmas.role: Supplies the average-consensus guarantee for PULM that underlies the theorem's assumed W-rate.

proof.description: For column ell of W, the diagonal anchor gives W_{ell,ell}^{(k)}=1/n, and row stochasticity rewrites each off-diagonal error as a convex sum over non-ell terms.
Stacking all rows except ell gives the submatrix recurrence labeled (12).
Taking infinity norms and using ||A_{-ell,-ell}^(k)||_infty<=1 shows the maximum column deviation is nonincreasing; then taking all columns gives monotonicity of max |W^(k)-E_n|.
Iterating (12) recurrently from Algorithm 1's W^(0)=I_n gives W_{-ell,ell}^{(0)}=0, hence the displayed product representation with initial vector -n^{-1}1_{n-1}.
Taking the Euclidean norm of the product representation gives the first printed inequality in (13), with the operator norm of the matrix product multiplying the vector norm.
Equation (13) continues by evaluating the vector norm factor as 1/sqrt(n) and then bounding the operator norm by the Frobenius norm.
For k>B and T=floor(k/B), decompose the product into full B-blocks and a leftover factor; Lemma 2 compares submatrix products with submatrices of full products.
Proposition 1 makes each block entry at least eta, so each block submatrix row sum is at most 1-eta; the proof derives a recursive maximum-entry contraction.
Multiplying the recursive inequalities and handling the leftover factor gives max product bounded by (1-eta)^T.
Continue (13), convert Frobenius norm to maximum entry, and obtain the column error bound.
Since the diagonal column error is identically zero, taking all columns gives the Frobenius W-error bound.
Define D^(k) from the diagonal of the half-step matrix and rewrite Algorithm 1 in compact matrix form.
Write the corresponding z-iteration and subtract W^(k+1)x to show the z-Wx error propagates linearly.
Consecutive multiplication and the initialization z_i^(0)=x_i, W^(0)=I_n give z^(k)=W^(k)x; combining with the W-error bound gives the PULM consensus error.
